title: CORAL: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens
one_liner: Use lightweight neural networks to read correctness signals buried in a language model's hidden layers at answer time, without retraining.
lead: Large language models are overconfident. They will happily declare a wrong answer with 90% certainty. Retraining the model to fix this is expensive. CORAL reads signals already hidden inside the model's calculations and steers it toward honest confidence at the moment of answering, using only tiny add-on networks that learn what 'correct' looks like.

paras: After tuning a language model to follow instructions and produce preferred answers, something breaks: the model becomes wildly overconfident. It assigns high certainty to wrong answers. This matters because downstream systems rely on the model's stated confidence — a recommendation system should distrust low-confidence predictions, but if the model lies about its confidence, the entire pipeline fails.

A naive fix is to retrain the model with a better confidence objective, but that costs compute time and can break the model's ability to answer correctly in the first place, because retraining involves changing all the weights simultaneously using backpropagation — a change meant to improve confidence can accidentally scramble the logic that produced the right answer. You are trapped: confident but wrong, or retrainable but expensive.

callout.html: A language model's confidence scores do not match how often it is actually right, and retraining to fix this is prohibitively expensive.

steps.b: Step 1: Pick a point to read
steps.text: At the moment the model generates its final answer, grab its internal layer-by-layer calculations.
Run the model on a small labeled set (correct / incorrect), keeping the hidden signals from each.
Fit lightweight neural networks to predict whether each example was correct, using only those hidden signals.
Blend the probes' predictions while penalizing large weights to prevent fitting to noise.
On new questions, run the probes and use their predictions to adjust the model's confidence score upward or downward.

paras: CORAL does not change the model's weights or rerun training. It adds a tiny module that sits outside the model and learns to read signals already present in the model's hidden activations (the intermediate numerical values the model computes as it processes). This module translates those signals into an honesty correction applied when the model answers a new question.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: distributed correctness signals
hidden.name: presence of correctness clues in hidden activations
paras: Before this paper, people assumed a model's confidence had to come from its final output layer — a single output that the model declares. CORAL discovers that information about whether an answer is correct or wrong is actually scattered across many layers and many hidden neurons. This is the paper's core insight: correctness is not broadcast from one place; it is distributed.

The paper measures this by training tiny neural networks (weight-decay probes) on each hidden layer independently, then combining their predictions. If layers far from the output can predict correctness, that proves the signal is distributed. The regularization (weight decay) ensures the probes learn general patterns, not memorized quirks.

heat.caption: Darker means more correctness signal. Distributed: many layers, not just the last.

reads.html: The model's internal math, layer by layer, contains clues about whether its answer will be right or wrong. These clues are not loud — no single neuron screams 'wrong' — but a small neural network can learn to read them.
Multi-layer activation-based probe predictions aggregate distributed correctness information using regularized MLPs, enabling calibration-aware steering without model retraining.

mechanism.h2: Why distributed signals work better than retraining
paras: Retraining the model changes its weights, which risks breaking the answer accuracy you fought to achieve. CORAL instead reads from activations (the numbers flowing through the model as it answers one question) without moving anything permanent. Because correctness information is scattered across layers, a single layer is not enough — no one place has the whole truth. Combining signals from many layers, with regularization to ignore noise, gives a reliable estimate of whether the current answer is likely correct.

The mechanism: as the model runs, each layer computes representations (lists of numbers) that encode what it understands so far. Correctness of the final answer leaves traces in these intermediate representations — the model's internal 'thinking.' The probes learn to read those traces. When answering a new question, the probes vote on correctness, and their combined vote steers the confidence score. This works because the probes only read; they do not interfere with the model's computation, so they cannot break accuracy.

stages.s: Model runs, collecting hidden activations from all layers
Probe at each layer predicts correctness from that layer alone
Combine predictions with regularization to weight reliable layers
Steering adjustment applied to final confidence score

math.words: The total steering loss is the sum of prediction errors across all probes, plus a penalty that pushes probe weights toward zero to prevent overfitting.
math.equation: L = sum_j (correctness_j - probe_j)^2 + lambda * sum_i w_i^2
symbols: whether example j was actually correct (1 or 0)
the probe's predicted probability that example j is correct
a weight inside the probe network
regularization strength: higher = more pushing weights toward zero

worked.title: A tiny worked example with 2 examples and one layer
lines: Example 1: correct answer. Probe predicted 0.6. Error = (1.0 - 0.6)^2 = 0.16.
Example 2: wrong answer. Probe predicted 0.7. Error = (0.0 - 0.7)^2 = 0.49.
Assume probe weights sum to w_1=0.8, w_2=0.3, w_3=0.5. Regularization penalty at lambda=0.1: 0.1 * (0.64 + 0.09 + 0.25) = 0.1 * 0.98 = 0.098.
Total loss = 0.65 + 0.098 = 0.748. The regularization term pushed all weights smaller.

math.note: The regularization term ensures the probe learns general patterns of correctness rather than memorizing noise unique to the training set.

bars.h2: The improvement compared to no steering

charts.title: No steering (baseline)
charts.note: The model is confident regardless of whether it is right. Calibration is poor.

charts.title: CORAL steering
charts.note: The model now separates right from wrong in its confidence. Calibration is honest.

items.html: If the probes train without weight decay, they memorize quirks of the training set rather than learning real correctness patterns. The regularization term prevents this by penalizing large weights, forcing the probes to stay simple.

If the calibration dataset is too small or skewed (e.g., all easy questions), the probes learn spurious patterns. The steering will fail on held-out benchmarks. A diverse calibration set is essential.
If the probes train on layers from a different model or during different reasoning patterns, they may not transfer. The paper addresses this by testing on held-out benchmarks.

Use moderate-sized calibration data, tune lambda via held-out validation, and apply the learned probes only to the same model family. The paper reports transfer across four benchmarks, proving this works when done correctly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny language model that gives answers to multiple-choice questions (e.g., a pretrained 3B model fine-tuned on a small QA task). Collect 200 examples with correct and incorrect labels. Train CORAL probes on half, then evaluate on the other half and on a separate held-out test set. Measure: Does the steering improve the correlation between the model's confidence and its actual accuracy? This correlation matters because when confidence matches reality, downstream systems can trust the model's predictions — low-confidence answers are actually more likely to be wrong, and high-confidence answers more likely to be right. Does it work on different types of questions or different model sizes?
demo.closing: The demo must show that even with modest calibration data and no retraining, the model's confidence score becomes honest — predictions marked high confidence are actually more often correct.
